title: A Full Response, Mostly Empty Receptors

scenes.tts: This tissue is responding at its maximum. Yet only about five percent of its receptors are occupied. The other ninety-five percent are empty. How can a tissue give a full response with almost all of its receptors empty?
scenes.visual: A row of twenty blue receptors on a membrane. Below, a response bar fills green to its maximum. One ligand lands on one receptor and a label reads 5% occupied; the other nineteen are marked empty. A large question mark rises over the row.
scenes.narration: This tissue is responding at its maximum. Yet only about five percent of its receptors are occupied. The other ninety-five percent are empty. How can a tissue give a full response with almost all of its receptors empty?

scenes.tts: To see why, start with binding. A ligand is any molecule that binds the receptor. The fraction of receptors occupied is the ligand concentration, divided by K d plus the ligand concentration. K d is the dissociation constant, the ligand concentration that fills half of the receptors. Five percent occupancy comes at a ligand concentration far below K d.
scenes.caption: To see why, start with binding. A ligand is any molecule that binds the receptor. The fraction of receptors occupied is the ligand concentration, divided by Kd plus the ligand concentration. Kd is the dissociation constant, the ligand concentration that fills half of the receptors. 5% occupancy comes at a ligand concentration far below Kd.
scenes.visual: The occupancy equation is written. A yellow S-shaped occupancy curve is drawn against log ligand concentration; a dot marks 50% where the axis reads Kd, then slides far to the left to mark 5%.
scenes.narration: To see why, start with binding. A ligand is any molecule that binds the receptor. The fraction of receptors occupied is the ligand concentration, divided by Kd plus the ligand concentration. Kd is the dissociation constant, the ligand concentration that fills half of the receptors. 5% occupancy comes at a ligand concentration far below Kd.

scenes.tts: Alfred Clark assumed that response is proportional to occupancy. The E C 50 is the concentration that gives half of the maximum response. With that assumption, the E C 50 would equal K d. But in 1956, Mark Nickerson reported that a tissue can reach its full response before all of its receptors are occupied.
scenes.caption: Alfred Clark assumed that response is proportional to occupancy. The EC50 is the concentration that gives half of the maximum response. With that assumption, the EC50 would equal Kd. But in 1956, Mark Nickerson reported that a tissue can reach its full response before all of its receptors are occupied.
scenes.visual: A green response curve is drawn exactly on top of the yellow occupancy curve; a green marker at half maximum falls on Kd. Then the green curve slides left of the yellow one and reaches its top while the yellow curve is still low.
scenes.narration: Alfred Clark assumed that response is proportional to occupancy. The EC50 is the concentration that gives half of the maximum response. With that assumption, the EC50 would equal Kd. But in 1956, Mark Nickerson reported that a tissue can reach its full response before all of its receptors are occupied.

scenes.tts: The reason is amplification in the pathway after the receptor. Picture a bottling line where the capper is the bottleneck. Once it runs at full speed, extra filling machines add nothing. Likewise, once enough receptors are occupied to saturate the slowest step downstream, more occupied receptors change nothing. The receptors that are not needed are called spare receptors. Together they make up the receptor reserve.
scenes.visual: The row of receptors returns with a pathway gauge below, labelled slowest step downstream. One ligand lands and the gauge fills to full speed. Four more ligands land and the gauge does not change. The other receptors are bracketed as spare receptors, then as the receptor reserve.
scenes.narration: The reason is amplification in the pathway after the receptor. Picture a bottling line where the capper is the bottleneck. Once it runs at full speed, extra filling machines add nothing. Likewise, once enough receptors are occupied to saturate the slowest step downstream, more occupied receptors change nothing. The receptors that are not needed are called spare receptors. Together they make up the receptor reserve.

scenes.tts: K d is a property of the receptor. The E C 50 is a property of the whole pathway. Say the pathway reaches its ceiling at five percent occupancy, and responds in proportion below that. Half of the maximum then needs only two and a half percent occupancy. That puts the E C 50 thirty-nine times below K d, with no change in binding.
scenes.caption: Kd is a property of the receptor. The EC50 is a property of the whole pathway. Say the pathway reaches its ceiling at 5% occupancy, and responds in proportion below that. Half of the maximum then needs only 2.5% occupancy. That puts the EC50 39 times below Kd, with no change in binding.
scenes.visual: Yellow occupancy curve with Kd marked. The green response curve is drawn, rising to its ceiling where the yellow curve reads 5%. A line at half the maximum drops to the axis at the EC50, and a bracket shows the gap to Kd as 39-fold.
scenes.narration: Kd is a property of the receptor. The EC50 is a property of the whole pathway. Say the pathway reaches its ceiling at 5% occupancy, and responds in proportion below that. Half of the maximum then needs only 2.5% occupancy. That puts the EC50 39 times below Kd, with no change in binding.

scenes.tts: You can prove a reserve by taking receptors away with an irreversible blocker. Remove half, and the curve moves right; remove ninety percent, and it moves further right. In this tissue, only when more than ninety-five percent are gone does the maximum fall. A real tissue has no sharp threshold, so the maximum sags gradually, but the order holds: shift first, fall later. Keep the rule: a full response does not mean every receptor is occupied.
scenes.caption: You can prove a reserve by taking receptors away with an irreversible blocker. Remove half, and the curve moves right; remove 90%, and it moves further right. In this tissue, only when more than 95% are gone does the maximum fall. A real tissue has no sharp threshold, so the maximum sags gradually, but the order holds: shift first, fall later. Keep the rule: a full response does not mean every receptor is occupied.
scenes.visual: The green response curve with a grey ghost of the original. A red label steps through half removed, 90% removed, more than 95% removed; each time the old curve clears and the new one is drawn, further right, and in the last case lower. The plot is labelled idealised.
scenes.narration: You can prove a reserve by taking receptors away with an irreversible blocker. Remove half, and the curve moves right; remove 90%, and it moves further right. In this tissue, only when more than 95% are gone does the maximum fall. A real tissue has no sharp threshold, so the maximum sags gradually, but the order holds: shift first, fall later. Keep the rule: a full response does not mean every receptor is occupied.
